props.title: Seven Days in May
props.initialSlug: Military plot to overthrow US president exposed

sections.content: Seven Days in May stands as one of Hollywood's most taut political thrillers, arriving at the height of Cold War tensions. Director John Frankenheimer, fresh off The Manchurian Candidate (1962), crafts another masterwork of paranoid cinema that explores a military coup attempt against a U.S. president. The film's timing was impeccable - releasing just months after JFK's assassination and during peak nuclear anxiety. Rod Serling's screenplay, adapted from the Fletcher Knebel novel, taps into very real fears about military overreach and constitutional crisis that resonated deeply with 1960s audiences.

sections.content: The film exists in fascinating dialogue with other political thrillers of the era. While Dr. Strangelove (1964) took a satirical approach to nuclear anxiety, and Fail Safe (1964) went for documentary-style realism, Seven Days in May charts a middle course - maintaining plausibility while ramping up the dramatic tension. Frankenheimer's direction is clinical and methodical, building suspense through procedural detail rather than action setpieces. The film's influence can be seen in later political thrillers like The Day of the Jackal (1973) and All the President's Men (1976).

The performances ground the film's extraordinary premise in reality. Burt Lancaster's General Scott is a charismatic but dangerous figure who believes he's saving democracy by destroying it - a character type that would influence countless later film villains. Kirk Douglas provides the moral center as Colonel Casey, torn between military loyalty and constitutional duty. Fredric March's President Lyman feels remarkably human and vulnerable - a stark contrast to how presidents were typically portrayed in Hollywood at the time. SUBHEAD: Cold War Cinema Context

sections.content: Seven Days in May marked a turning point in how Hollywood depicted the military-industrial complex. While 1950s films generally portrayed the military as heroes defending against communist threats, the 1960s saw more critical examinations. This film, along with Dr. Strangelove (1964) and Fail Safe (1964), formed a trilogy of 1964 releases that questioned military authority and nuclear policy. The film's themes would later be echoed in works like The Package (1989) and Crimson Tide (1995).
